claim: Protein-DNA complexes can impede DNA replication and cause replication fork collapse.
source: Protein-DNA complexes can impede DNA replication and cause replication fork collapse.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about replication fork barriers.

claim: Homologous recombination is deployed to restart replication when protein-DNA complexes cause replication fork collapse.
source: Whilst it is known that homologous recombination is deployed in such instances to restart replication, it is unclear how a stalled fork transitions into a collapsed fork at which recombination proteins can load.
evidence: This is stated as known information in the field.

claim: It is unclear how a stalled fork transitions into a collapsed fork at which recombination proteins can load.
source: Whilst it is known that homologous recombination is deployed in such instances to restart replication, it is unclear how a stalled fork transitions into a collapsed fork at which recombination proteins can load.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: Assays in Schizosaccharomyces pombe for studying recombination induced by replication fork collapse at RTS1 were previously established.
source: Previously we established assays in Schizosaccharomyces pombe for studying recombination induced by replication fork collapse at the site-specific protein-DNA barrier RTS1 (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Efficient recruitment/retention of Rad51 and Rad52 to RTS1 depends on unloading of PCNA from DNA by Elg1.
source: Here, we provide evidence that efficient recruitment/retention of two key recombination proteins (Rad51 and Rad52) to RTS1 depends on unloading of the polymerase sliding clamp PCNA from DNA by Elg1.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of Elg1, reduced recombination is partially suppressed by deleting fbh1.
source: We also show that, in the absence of Elg1, reduced recombination is partially suppressed by deleting fbh1 or, to a lesser extent, srs2, which encode known anti-recombinogenic DNA helicases.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of Elg1, reduced recombination is partially suppressed by deleting srs2 to a lesser extent than fbh1.
source: We also show that, in the absence of Elg1, reduced recombination is partially suppressed by deleting fbh1 or, to a lesser extent, srs2, which encode known anti-recombinogenic DNA helicases.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Fbh1 and Srs2 encode known anti-recombinogenic DNA helicases.
source: We also show that, in the absence of Elg1, reduced recombination is partially suppressed by deleting fbh1 or, to a lesser extent, srs2, which encode known anti-recombinogenic DNA helicases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: PCNA unloading by Elg1 is necessary to limit Fbh1 and Srs2 activity and thereby enable recombination to proceed.
source: These findings suggest that PCNA unloading by Elg1 is necessary to limit Fbh1 and Srs2 activity, and thereby enable recombination to proceed.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Replication failure is a major cause of cancer and other pathological states through loss of genome integrity and catastrophic chromosomal rearrangements.
source: Replication failure is a major cause of cancer and other pathological states through loss of genome integrity and catastrophic chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Protein-DNA complexes stall replication forks by physically impeding the CMG replicative helicase.
source: Major hurdles to the successful completion of DNA replication include protein-DNA complexes that stall replication forks by physically impeding the Cdc45-MCM2-7-GINS (CMG) replicative helicase (Lambert and Carr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: CMG can overcome stalling with the help of an additional helicase and the Fork Protection Complex.
source: In some cases CMG overcomes stalling, with the help of an additional helicase and the Fork Protection Complex, with the latter ensuring that the replication proteins at the fork (collectively known as the replisome) are maintained in a state that is competent to resume DNA synthesis (Azvolinsky et al., 2006; Errico and Costanzo, 2012; Ivessa et al., 2003; Leman and Noguchi, 2012; Sabouri et al., 2012; Sofueva et al., 2011; Steinacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The Fork Protection Complex ensures that the replisome is maintained in a state that is competent to resume DNA synthesis.
source: In some cases CMG overcomes stalling, with the help of an additional helicase and the Fork Protection Complex, with the latter ensuring that the replication proteins at the fork (collectively known as the replisome) are maintained in a state that is competent to resume DNA synthesis (Azvolinsky et al., 2006; Errico and Costanzo, 2012; Ivessa et al., 2003; Leman and Noguchi, 2012; Sabouri et al., 2012; Sofueva et al., 2011; Steinacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Replication forks can be inhibited from catalysing further DNA synthesis through a process termed fork collapse.
source: However, despite these measures, replication forks can be inhibited from catalysing further DNA synthesis through a process termed fork collapse (Cortez, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Fork collapse involves remodelling or disassembly of the replisome and sometimes DNA breakage.
source: This poorly understood process involves remodelling or disassembly of the replisome and sometimes DNA breakage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about fork collapse.

claim: At RTS1 in fission yeast, fork collapse appears to be an inevitable consequence of replication fork stalling.
source: At some strong replication fork barriers (RFBs), such as RTS1 in fission yeast, fork collapse appears to be an inevitable consequence of replication fork stalling, and results in the recruitment of homologous recombination (HR) proteins that restart replication (Lambert et al., 2010; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fork collapse at RTS1 results in the recruitment of HR proteins that restart replication.
source: At some strong replication fork barriers (RFBs), such as RTS1 in fission yeast, fork collapse appears to be an inevitable consequence of replication fork stalling, and results in the recruitment of homologous recombination (HR) proteins that restart replication (Lambert et al., 2010; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recombination-dependent replication is thought to be important for ensuring the timely completion of genome duplication.
source: This recombination-dependent replication (RDR) is thought to be important for ensuring the timely completion of genome duplication, helping to avoid chromosome breakage and missegregation that could otherwise occur during mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of RDR.

claim: RDR helps to avoid chromosome breakage and missegregation that could otherwise occur during mitosis.
source: This recombination-dependent replication (RDR) is thought to be important for ensuring the timely completion of genome duplication, helping to avoid chromosome breakage and missegregation that could otherwise occur during mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of RDR.

claim: A central step in RDR is the invasion of a duplex DNA by a homologous single-stranded DNA catalysed by Rad51.
source: A central step in RDR is the invasion of a duplex DNA by a homologous single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) catalysed by the HR protein Rad51 (Anand et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Rad51-catalyzed strand invasion reaction forms a D-loop at which replication proteins are thought to reassemble.
source: This reaction forms a displacement (D)-loop at which replication proteins are thought to reassemble (Lydeard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rad52 aids RDR by mediating the loading of Rad51 onto ssDNA coated with RPA.
source: Rad52 aids this process by mediating the loading of Rad51 onto ssDNA coated with the ssDNA binding protein RPA (Krogh and Symington, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rad52 helps protect Rad51-ssDNA filaments from disruption by Srs2 and Fbh1.
source: It also helps protect Rad51-ssDNA filaments from disruption by the anti-recombinogenic DNA helicases Srs2 and Fbh1 (Lorenz et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2018; Osman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rad51 and Rad52 are recruited to RTS1 within minutes of replication fork stalling.
source: In our earlier work we showed that Rad51 and Rad52 are recruited to RTS1 within minutes of replication fork stalling, giving rise to restarted replication that is prone to template switching (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Restarted replication at RTS1 is prone to template switching.
source: In our earlier work we showed that Rad51 and Rad52 are recruited to RTS1 within minutes of replication fork stalling, giving rise to restarted replication that is prone to template switching (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Little is known about what steps are required for the stalled replication fork to transition into a collapsed fork at which Rad51 and Rad52 can efficiently load.
source: However, little is known about what steps are required for the stalled replication fork to transition into a collapsed fork at which Rad51 and Rad52 can efficiently load.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Some disassembly and/or re-organization of the replisome is presumably required so that HR proteins can gain access to the DNA.
source: Presumably some disassembly and/or re-organization of the replisome is required so that HR proteins can gain access to the DNA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on logical reasoning.

claim: PCNA is a core component of the replisome.
source: One of the core components of the replisome is the homotrimeric ring-shaped complex PCNA, which acts as a sliding clamp for the DNA polymerases, and scaffold for the dynamic recruitment of various proteins that promote replication and repair (Choe and Moldovan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PCNA acts as a sliding clamp for the DNA polymerases.
source: One of the core components of the replisome is the homotrimeric ring-shaped complex PCNA, which acts as a sliding clamp for the DNA polymerases, and scaffold for the dynamic recruitment of various proteins that promote replication and repair (Choe and Moldovan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PCNA acts as a scaffold for the dynamic recruitment of various proteins that promote replication and repair.
source: One of the core components of the replisome is the homotrimeric ring-shaped complex PCNA, which acts as a sliding clamp for the DNA polymerases, and scaffold for the dynamic recruitment of various proteins that promote replication and repair (Choe and Moldovan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PCNA has to be actively unloaded from chromosomes following both the completion of each Okazaki fragment and termination of replication.
source: As PCNA encircles DNA it has to be actively unloaded from chromosomes following both the completion of each Okazaki fragment and termination of replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA function.

claim: It is unknown whether PCNA has to be unloaded for recombination to occur at a stalled/collapsed replication fork.
source: However, it is unknown whether PCNA has to be unloaded for recombination to occur at a stalled/collapsed replication fork.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: Elg1 (ATAD5 in humans) is a principle factor for unloading PCNA.
source: A principle factor for unloading PCNA is Elg1 (ATAD5 in humans) (Kubota et al., 2013a; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Elg1/ATAD5 forms a replication factor C (RFC)-like complex with Rfc2-5.
source: Elg1/ATAD5 forms a replication factor C (RFC)-like complex with Rfc2-5 (Bellaoui et al., 2003; Ben-Aroya et al., 2003; Kanellis et al., 2003), which is vital for genome stability, and, in mice and humans, appears to act as a tumour suppressor (Bell et al., 2011; Gazy et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2016; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016; Shemesh et al., 2017; Sikdar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Elg1-Rfc2-5 complex is vital for genome stability.
source: Elg1/ATAD5 forms a replication factor C (RFC)-like complex with Rfc2-5 (Bellaoui et al., 2003; Ben-Aroya et al., 2003; Kanellis et al., 2003), which is vital for genome stability, and, in mice and humans, appears to act as a tumour suppressor (Bell et al., 2011; Gazy et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2016; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016; Shemesh et al., 2017; Sikdar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mice and humans, Elg1/ATAD5 appears to act as a tumour suppressor.
source: Elg1/ATAD5 forms a replication factor C (RFC)-like complex with Rfc2-5 (Bellaoui et al., 2003; Ben-Aroya et al., 2003; Kanellis et al., 2003), which is vital for genome stability, and, in mice and humans, appears to act as a tumour suppressor (Bell et al., 2011; Gazy et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2016; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016; Shemesh et al., 2017; Sikdar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fission yeast lacking Elg1 exhibit reduced levels of RTS1-induced recombination.
source: Here we discover that fission yeast lacking Elg1 exhibit reduced levels of RTS1-induced recombination and fewer cells with Rad51 and Rad52 foci colocalizing with RTS1.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Fission yeast lacking Elg1 have fewer cells with Rad51 and Rad52 foci colocalizing with RTS1.
source: Here we discover that fission yeast lacking Elg1 exhibit reduced levels of RTS1-induced recombination and fewer cells with Rad51 and Rad52 foci colocalizing with RTS1.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The hypo-recombination in an elg1∆ mutant is fully suppressed by a mutation rendering PCNA prone to disassembly.
source: We also show that the hypo-recombination in an elg1∆ mutant is fully suppressed by a mutation rendering PCNA prone to disassembly, and partially suppressed by deleting either fbh1 or srs2.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: RTS1 is inserted between a direct repeat of mutant ade6- heteroalleles on chromosome 3 in the standard assay.
source: In our standard assay, RTS1 is inserted between a direct repeat of mutant ade6- heteroalleles on chromosome 3 (the '0 kb site') so that recombination can be measured by determining the frequency of two types of ade6+ recombinants (gene conversions and deletions) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup shown in Figure 1.

claim: Recombination can be measured by determining the frequency of two types of ade6+ recombinants (gene conversions and deletions).
source: In our standard assay, RTS1 is inserted between a direct repeat of mutant ade6- heteroalleles on chromosome 3 (the '0 kb site') so that recombination can be measured by determining the frequency of two types of ade6+ recombinants (gene conversions and deletions) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method shown in Figure 1.

claim: RTS1 is a polar RFB.
source: As RTS1 is a polar RFB, and the ade6 locus is replicated with a strong directional bias (telomere to centromere), only one orientation of the barrier blocks forks at this genomic location, which we refer to as the active orientation (AO) (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ade6 locus is replicated with a strong directional bias (telomere to centromere).
source: As RTS1 is a polar RFB, and the ade6 locus is replicated with a strong directional bias (telomere to centromere), only one orientation of the barrier blocks forks at this genomic location, which we refer to as the active orientation (AO) (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Only one orientation of RTS1 blocks forks at the ade6 genomic location, which is referred to as the active orientation (AO).
source: As RTS1 is a polar RFB, and the ade6 locus is replicated with a strong directional bias (telomere to centromere), only one orientation of the barrier blocks forks at this genomic location, which we refer to as the active orientation (AO) (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The inactive orientation (IO) of RTS1 does not block replication.
source: The opposite orientation, which does not block replication, is called the inactive orientation (IO).
evidence: This is a definition based on experimental observations.

claim: The inactive barrier (RTS1-IO) has no effect on the frequency of recombination.
source: A comparison of the frequency of ade6+ recombinants in strains with and without RTS1-IO shows that the inactive barrier has no effect on the frequency of recombination (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTS1-AO strongly induces recombination.
source: In contrast, RTS1-AO strongly induces recombination (Nguyen et al., 2015) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: A fission yeast elg1∆ mutant containing RTS1-IO exhibits slightly higher levels of spontaneous recombination than a wild-type strain with RTS1-IO.
source: In line with the observation that an elg1∆ mutant exhibits increased spontaneous direct repeat recombination in budding yeast (Gazy et al., 2013), a fission yeast elg1∆ mutant containing RTS1-IO exhibits slightly higher levels of spontaneous recombination than a wild-type strain with RTS1-IO, suggesting that Elg1 has an anti-recombinogenic function (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and a citation to prior work in budding yeast.

claim: Elg1 has an anti-recombinogenic function.
source: In line with the observation that an elg1∆ mutant exhibits increased spontaneous direct repeat recombination in budding yeast (Gazy et al., 2013), a fission yeast elg1∆ mutant containing RTS1-IO exhibits slightly higher levels of spontaneous recombination than a wild-type strain with RTS1-IO, suggesting that Elg1 has an anti-recombinogenic function (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: The modest increase in spontaneous recombination in elg1∆ is not observed in all genetic backgrounds.
source: However, this modest increase in recombination is not observed in all genetic backgrounds (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: The elevated levels of recombination in wild-type strains containing RTS1-AO are reduced dramatically in an elg1∆ mutant, with gene conversions down ~20 fold and deletions down ~4 fold.
source: In stark contrast to the modest increase in spontaneous recombination, the elevated levels of recombination in wild-type strains containing RTS1-AO are reduced dramatically in an elg1∆ mutant, with gene conversions down ~20 fold and deletions down ~4 fold (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: The reductions in recombination in elg1∆ are not caused by any weakening of the RTS1 barrier.
source: These reductions are not caused by any weakening of the RTS1 barrier, as native two-dimensional gel electrophoretic (2DGE) analysis of replication intermediates shows similar levels of blocked replication forks in wild-type and elg1∆ strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2DGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Native 2DGE analysis of replication intermediates shows similar levels of blocked replication forks in wild-type and elg1∆ strains.
source: These reductions are not caused by any weakening of the RTS1 barrier, as native two-dimensional gel electrophoretic (2DGE) analysis of replication intermediates shows similar levels of blocked replication forks in wild-type and elg1∆ strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2DGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Elg1 generally causes increased spontaneous recombination in budding yeast.
source: Previous studies in budding yeast have shown that loss of Elg1 generally causes increased spontaneous recombination (Ben-Aroya et al., 2003), however, recombination induced by methylmethane sulfonate (MMS) and phleomycin, which cause lesions that can impede replication forks, was reported to be reduced in an elg1∆ mutant (Ogiwara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recombination induced by MMS and phleomycin was reported to be reduced in an elg1∆ mutant in budding yeast.
source: Previous studies in budding yeast have shown that loss of Elg1 generally causes increased spontaneous recombination (Ben-Aroya et al., 2003), however, recombination induced by methylmethane sulfonate (MMS) and phleomycin, which cause lesions that can impede replication forks, was reported to be reduced in an elg1∆ mutant (Ogiwara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MMS and phleomycin cause lesions that can impede replication forks.
source: Previous studies in budding yeast have shown that loss of Elg1 generally causes increased spontaneous recombination (Ben-Aroya et al., 2003), however, recombination induced by methylmethane sulfonate (MMS) and phleomycin, which cause lesions that can impede replication forks, was reported to be reduced in an elg1∆ mutant (Ogiwara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these agents.

claim: Elg1 has a pro-recombinogenic function that is specifically required to promote RFB-induced recombination.
source: Our data show that Elg1, in addition to having an anti-recombinogenic function, also has a pro-recombinogenic function that is specifically required to promote RFB-induced recombination, which likely explains the reduction in MMS/phleomycin-induced recombination observed previously in budding yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and prior observations.

claim: The reduction in MMS/phleomycin-induced recombination in budding yeast elg1∆ is likely explained by Elg1's pro-recombinogenic function at RFBs.
source: Our data show that Elg1, in addition to having an anti-recombinogenic function, also has a pro-recombinogenic function that is specifically required to promote RFB-induced recombination, which likely explains the reduction in MMS/phleomycin-induced recombination observed previously in budding yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and prior observations.

claim: RDR triggered by RTS1-AO exhibits a high frequency of template switching downstream of the barrier.
source: RDR, triggered by RTS1-AO, exhibits a high frequency of template switching (TS) downstream of the barrier, which can be measured using the ade6- direct repeat recombination reporter (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1.

claim: Template switching can be measured using the ade6- direct repeat recombination reporter.
source: RDR, triggered by RTS1-AO, exhibits a high frequency of template switching (TS) downstream of the barrier, which can be measured using the ade6- direct repeat recombination reporter (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1.

claim: Gene conversions and deletions at the 12.4 kb site were reduced in an elg1∆ mutant by ~5 fold and ~6 fold, respectively.
source: Gene conversions and deletions were reduced in an elg1∆ mutant by ~5 fold and ~6 fold, respectively, with the former being suppressed to spontaneous levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: Gene conversions at the 12.4 kb site in an elg1∆ mutant are suppressed to spontaneous levels.
source: Gene conversions and deletions were reduced in an elg1∆ mutant by ~5 fold and ~6 fold, respectively, with the former being suppressed to spontaneous levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: Elg1 promotes template switching associated with restarted replication.
source: These data show that Elg1 promotes TS associated with restarted replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on template switching.

claim: Even in wild-type cells, only a minority of restarted replication reaches the reporter 12.4 kb downstream of RTS1-AO to register a TS event.
source: We have previously shown that, even in wild-type cells, only a minority of restarted replication reaches the reporter 12.4 kb downstream of RTS1-AO to register a TS event (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Deleting the strongest centromere-proximal origin (ori-1253) provides more time for RDR to reach the downstream reporter leading to a dramatic increase in TS.
source: We have also shown that deleting the strongest centromere-proximal origin (ori-1253) provides more time for RDR to reach the downstream reporter leading to a dramatic increase in TS (Jalan et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of ori-1253 in the wild-type resulted in a ~21 fold increase in gene conversions and a ~13 fold increase in deletions.
source: In line with previous data (Nguyen et al., 2015), deletion of ori-1253 in the wild-type resulted in a ~21 fold increase in gene conversions and a ~13 fold increase in deletions (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E,F and a citation to prior work.

claim: In an elg1∆ mutant with ori-1253 deleted, the increase in recombination was only ~6 fold for gene conversions and ~7 fold for deletions.
source: In contrast, the increase in an elg1∆ mutant was only ~6 fold for gene conversions and ~7 fold for deletions (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The data suggest that Elg1 promotes the kinetics of TS and/or efficient RDR.
source: Whilst not discounting the possibility that Elg1 affects restarted replication stability, these data suggest that Elg1 promotes the kinetics of TS and/or efficient RDR.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on ori-1253 deletion.

claim: A deficiency in RDR is not evident from 2DGE analysis of replication intermediates at RTS1-AO, as both wild-type and elg1∆ mutant exhibit similar levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules.
source: However, a deficiency in RDR is not evident from our 2DGE analysis of replication intermediates at RTS1-AO, as both wild-type and elg1∆ mutant exhibit similar levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules (representative of replication past the barrier, and fork convergence at the barrier, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by 2DGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Large Y-shaped DNA molecules are representative of replication past the barrier.
source: However, a deficiency in RDR is not evident from our 2DGE analysis of replication intermediates at RTS1-AO, as both wild-type and elg1∆ mutant exhibit similar levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules (representative of replication past the barrier, and fork convergence at the barrier, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of 2DGE data.

claim: Double Y-shaped DNA molecules are representative of fork convergence at the barrier.
source: However, a deficiency in RDR is not evident from our 2DGE analysis of replication intermediates at RTS1-AO, as both wild-type and elg1∆ mutant exhibit similar levels of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules (representative of replication past the barrier, and fork convergence at the barrier, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of 2DGE data.

claim: The data suggest that Elg1 is required for the TS process itself.
source: By a process of elimination, these data suggest that Elg1 is required for the TS process itself, although this conclusion assumes that 2DGE analysis provides an accurate measure of RDR efficiency, which may not always be true (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data, with caveats noted.

claim: 2DGE analysis does not provide a definitive measure of replication restart efficiency because the accumulation of replication intermediates depends on both their frequency and half-life within the cell population.
source: 2DGE analysis does not provide a definitive measure of replication restart efficiency because the accumulation of replication intermediates, within the DNA restriction fragment being analysed, depends on both their frequency and half-life within the cell population.
evidence: This is a logical explanation of the limitations of 2DGE analysis.

claim: A reduction in velocity of restarted replication could offset the effect of a reduced frequency of restarted forks in 2DGE analysis.
source: For example, a reduction in velocity of restarted replication could offset the effect of a reduced frequency of restarted forks (i.e. even though fewer cells within a population contain a restarted fork, those that do are more likely to contain one that resides within the restriction fragment at the point of analysis, resulting in little or no apparent change in the amount of large Y-shaped DNA molecules that are detected).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of how 2DGE results could be misleading.

claim: An increase in the frequency of fork convergence at the RFB could be offset by an increase in the speed with which converging forks are processed in 2DGE analysis.
source: Similarly, an increase in the frequency of fork convergence at the RFB (which would normally lead to a relative increase in large Y-shaped DNA molecules) could be offset by an increase in the speed with which converging forks are processed.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of how 2DGE results could be misleading.

claim: The absence of any apparent difference between wild-type and elg1∆ mutant in the accumulation of replication intermediates at around RTS1-AO does not rule out the possibility that RDR is deficient in an elg1∆ mutant.
source: Therefore, the absence of any apparent difference between wild-type and elg1∆ mutant in the accumulation of replication intermediates at around RTS1-AO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), does not rule out the possibility that RDR is deficient in an elg1∆ mutant (e.g. if fork convergence is faster, and restarted replication is slower, in an elg1∆ mutant, then this could result in no apparent change in the relative amount of large Y-shaped and double Y-shaped DNA molecules compared to wild-type).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the 2DGE data.

claim: The possibility that Elg1 promotes RDR and, in so-doing, drives TS at the 12.4 kb reporter cannot be excluded.
source: Taking this into account, we cannot exclude the possibility that Elg1 promotes RDR and, in so-doing, drives TS at the 12.4 kb reporter.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging an alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: Four characteristic patterns of CFP-PCNA nuclear fluorescence during the cell cycle have been described.
source: Four characteristic patterns of CFP-PCNA nuclear fluorescence during the cell cycle have been described (Meister et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Prior to S-phase, CFP-PCNA fluorescence is weak and diffuse, and occupies mainly the non-nucleolar part of the nucleus in wild-type cells.
source: Prior to S-phase the fluorescence is weak and diffuse, and occupies mainly the non-nucleolar part of the nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A.

claim: Between 10–15 min post anaphase bright CFP-PCNA foci appear marking the start of S-phase (pattern a) in wild-type cells.
source: Between 10–15 min post anaphase bright foci appear marking the start of S-phase (pattern a), which within ~5 min spread to fill much of the extranucleolar space (pattern b) (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: Within ~5 min of pattern a, CFP-PCNA fluorescence spreads to fill much of the extranucleolar space (pattern b) in wild-type cells.
source: Between 10–15 min post anaphase bright foci appear marking the start of S-phase (pattern a), which within ~5 min spread to fill much of the extranucleolar space (pattern b) (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: After ~20–25 min the bright CFP-PCNA fluorescence resolves into a slightly dimmer and more punctate pattern with fewer foci (pattern c) in wild-type cells.
source: After ~20–25 min the bright fluorescence resolves into a slightly dimmer and more punctate pattern with fewer foci (pattern c), and then after another ~15–20 min transitions to only one or two foci at the edges of the nucleolus (pattern d) (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: After another ~15–20 min, CFP-PCNA fluorescence transitions to only one or two foci at the edges of the nucleolus (pattern d) in wild-type cells.
source: After ~20–25 min the bright fluorescence resolves into a slightly dimmer and more punctate pattern with fewer foci (pattern c), and then after another ~15–20 min transitions to only one or two foci at the edges of the nucleolus (pattern d) (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: By ~60 min CFP-PCNA fluorescence returns to its pre-S-phase level in wild-type cells.
source: By ~60 min ﻿CFP-PCNA fluorescence returns to its pre-S-phase level.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2.

claim: In an elg1∆ mutant, CFP-PCNA patterns a – c appear similar to wild-type, albeit patterns b and c persist slightly longer.
source: In an elg1∆ mutant patterns a – c appear similar to wild-type, albeit patterns b and c persist slightly longer (Figure 2A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,B,D.

claim: In an elg1∆ mutant, pattern c does not transition into pattern d; instead ~30–40 min after the start of S-phase a new pattern of fluorescence emerges (pattern c*), which is characterised by large patches of very bright fluorescence.
source: However, unlike wild-type, pattern c does not transition into pattern d, instead ~30–40 min after the start of S-phase a new pattern of fluorescence emerges, which is characterised by large patches of very bright fluorescence (pattern c*).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,D.

claim: Pattern c* persists for up to ~40 min before changing into something that is more akin to pattern d in an elg1∆ mutant.
source: These persist for up to ~40 min before changing into something that is more akin to pattern d (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A,D.

claim: The start of S-phase is not delayed in an elg1∆ mutant.
source: Altogether these data show that the start of S-phase is not delayed in an elg1∆ mutant.

claim: The persistence of PCNA foci at later time points in elg1∆ mutant cells suggests a deficiency in PCNA removal from DNA.

claim: The D150E mutation in budding yeast PCNA rescues MMS sensitivity, hyper-sister chromatid recombination and telomere elongation in an elg1∆ mutant.
source: One such mutation is D150E, which rescues MMS sensitivity, hyper-sister chromatid recombination and telomere elongation in a budding yeast elg1∆ mutant (Johnson et al., 2016).

claim: The pcn1D150E mutant strain was viable and exhibited similar growth to the wild-type parental strain.

claim: Spontaneous recombination was increased 2–3-fold in the pcn1+ strain compared to the standard wild-type strain.
source: Spontaneous recombination was increased 2–3-fold in the pcn1+ strain compared to our standard wild-type strain (compare data in Figures 1C and 3A), suggesting that the presence of the linked natMX4 marker might be affecting pcn1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1C and 3A.

claim: The presence of the linked natMX4 marker might be affecting pcn1 expression.
source: Spontaneous recombination was increased 2–3-fold in the pcn1+ strain compared to our standard wild-type strain (compare data in Figures 1C and 3A), suggesting that the presence of the linked natMX4 marker might be affecting pcn1 expression.

claim: The pcn1D150E mutant exhibited an even higher frequency of recombination than the pcn1+ strain, which was 2–3-fold more.
source: Interestingly, the pcn1D150E mutant exhibited an even higher frequency of recombination, which was 2–3-fold more than the pcn1+ strain (Figure 1C).

claim: Proper retention of PCNA on DNA is important for suppressing spontaneous recombination.
source: This suggests that proper retention of PCNA on DNA is important for suppressing spontaneous recombination.

claim: Deletion of elg1 in a pcn1+ strain containing RTS1-AO results in a ~9 fold decrease in gene conversions and a ~3 fold decrease in deletions.
source: However, similar to the data in Figure 1D, deletion of elg1 in a pcn1+ strain containing RTS1-AO results in a ~9 fold decrease in gene conversions and a ~3 fold decrease in deletions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: Deleting elg1 in a pcn1D150E strain causes no reduction in recombination.
source: In contrast, deleting elg1 in a pcn1D150E strain causes no reduction in recombination (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: The data strongly suggest that Elg1 promotes RTS1-induced recombination through its ability to unload PCNA from DNA.
source: These data strongly suggest that Elg1 promotes RTS1-induced recombination through its ability to unload PCNA from DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on pcn1D150E suppression.

claim: In budding yeast, the Srs2 DNA helicase is recruited to stalled replication forks by SUMOylated PCNA.
source: In budding yeast, the Srs2 DNA helicase is recruited to stalled replication forks by SUMOylated PCNA, where it can limit recombination by disrupting Rad51-DNA filaments (Motegi et al., 2006; Papouli et al., 2005; Pfander et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Srs2 can limit recombination by disrupting Rad51-DNA filaments.
source: In budding yeast, the Srs2 DNA helicase is recruited to stalled replication forks by SUMOylated PCNA, where it can limit recombination by disrupting Rad51-DNA filaments (Motegi et al., 2006; Papouli et al., 2005; Pfander et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SUMO-like domain-containing protein Esc2 directs Srs2 turnover by the SUMO targeted ubiquitin ligase Slx5-Slx8 in budding yeast.
source: To achieve the right level of Srs2 activity, so that beneficial recombination proceeds whilst toxic recombination is kept in check, the SUMO-like domain-containing protein Esc2 directs Srs2 turnover by the SUMO targeted ubiquitin ligase Slx5-Slx8 (Urulangodi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Esc2 helps retain Elg1 at sites of replication stress and may limit the concentration of Srs2 at the blocked fork by promoting PCNA unloading.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It remains unknown how Srs2 is recruited to stalled replication forks in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast it remains unknown how Srs2 is recruited to stalled replication forks.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: A srs2∆ mutant exhibits greatly increased levels of RTS1-induced recombination.

source: This fold reduction in deletions is approximately the same as in a srs2+ background, however, the reduction in gene conversions is noticeably less (~13 fold versus ~20 fold).

claim: The reduction in gene conversions in a srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant is noticeably less than in a srs2+ elg1∆ mutant (~13 fold versus ~20 fold).
source: This fold reduction in deletions is approximately the same as in a srs2+ background, however, the reduction in gene conversions is noticeably less (~13 fold versus ~20 fold).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing experimental data.

claim: Srs2 is partly responsible for the reduction in gene conversions in an elg1∆ mutant.
source: This suggests that Srs2 is partly responsible for the reduction in gene conversions in an elg1∆ mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on the srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant.

claim: Much of the hyper-recombination in a srs2∆ mutant is still suppressed by deletion of elg1, indicating that Elg1's pro-recombinogenic function is mostly independent of limiting Srs2 activity.
source: However, the fact that much of the hyper-recombination in a srs2∆ mutant is still suppressed by deletion of elg1 indicates that Elg1's pro-recombinogenic function is mostly independent of limiting Srs2 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on the srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant.

claim: A srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant in budding yeast exhibits impaired growth and a synergistic increase in sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, including MMS and CPT.
source: In budding yeast, a srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant exhibits impaired growth and a synergistic increase in sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, including MMS and the Topoisomerase I inhibitor camptothecin (CPT), which causes replication fork breakage (Gazy et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CPT is a Topoisomerase I inhibitor which causes replication fork breakage.
source: In budding yeast, a srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant exhibits impaired growth and a synergistic increase in sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, including MMS and the Topoisomerase I inhibitor camptothecin (CPT), which causes replication fork breakage (Gazy et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CPT.

claim: A fission yeast srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant exhibits a synergistic increase in sensitivity to MMS.
source: In contrast, a fission yeast srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant, although exhibiting a synergistic increase in sensitivity to MMS, exhibits no obvious deficiency in growth and a CPT sensitivity that is the same as a srs2∆ single mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: A fission yeast srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant exhibits no obvious deficiency in growth.
source: In contrast, a fission yeast srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant, although exhibiting a synergistic increase in sensitivity to MMS, exhibits no obvious deficiency in growth and a CPT sensitivity that is the same as a srs2∆ single mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: A fission yeast srs2∆ elg1∆ double mutant has a CPT sensitivity that is the same as a srs2∆ single mutant.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

source: Therefore, the differences in recombination between single and double mutant strains is unlikely to stem from a difference in their growth and viability.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similar to Srs2, Fbh1 limits Rad51-dependent recombination at blocked replication forks by disrupting Rad51-DNA filaments.
source: Similar to Srs2, Fbh1 limits Rad51-dependent recombination at blocked replication forks by disrupting Rad51-DNA filaments (Lorenz et al., 2009; Simandlova et al., 2013; Tsutsui et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fbh1 is part of an E3 ligase complex that ubiquitinates Rad51 to target it for degradation.
source: It is also part of an E3 ligase complex that ubiquitinates Rad51 to target it for degradation (Chu et al., 2015; Tsutsui et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: In humans, Fbh1 is recruited to sites of DNA replication and damage by interaction with PCNA mediated by two PCNA-binding motifs (an N-terminal PIP-box and C-terminal APIM) (Bacquin et al., 2013).

claim: An fbh1∆ single mutant exhibits impaired growth relative to wild-type.
source: An fbh1∆ single mutant exhibits impaired growth relative to wild-type (Osman et al., 2005), which is not exacerbated by deletion of elg1.

claim: The impaired growth of an fbh1∆ single mutant is not exacerbated by deletion of elg1.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fold reduction in deletions upon Fbh1 overexpression is the same as in an elg1∆ mutant (~4 fold).
source: We have shown previously that overexpressing Fbh1, with its helicase activity intact, is sufficient to suppress RTS1-induced recombination and, interestingly, the fold reduction in deletions is the same as in an elg1∆ mutant (~4 fold), with the reduction in gene conversions being slightly less (~7 fold versus ~20 fold in an elg1∆ mutant) (Lorenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and comparison with current data.

claim: The reduction in gene conversions upon Fbh1 overexpression is slightly less than in an elg1∆ mutant (~7 fold versus ~20 fold).
source: We have shown previously that overexpressing Fbh1, with its helicase activity intact, is sufficient to suppress RTS1-induced recombination and, interestingly, the fold reduction in deletions is the same as in an elg1∆ mutant (~4 fold), with the reduction in gene conversions being slightly less (~7 fold versus ~20 fold in an elg1∆ mutant) (Lorenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and comparison with current data.
